item.passage:
Lena Osei wrote out every word of her rebuttals. At the Tuesday practices of the Carver Middle School debate team, she arrived with a stack of index cards held together by a rubber band, each card numbered in one corner and filled on both sides, and she read them in order. She won more rounds than she lost that way. Her partner, Tomas Reyes, wrote nothing out ahead of time. He kept the flow: a long sheet of paper folded into columns, on which he took down every argument the other team made, in a private shorthand of arrows and circled letters.

"You're answering the round you expected," he told her after one practice in February, tapping her cards with his pen. "Not the round you're in." He had said the same thing, in nearly the same words, at least four times since November. Lately, when she pulled the rubber band off her cards before a practice round, he put his forehead down on the table.

The regional final was held on a Saturday in the library at Westbrook High. The resolution was that towns should end late fees at their public libraries, and Carver had drawn the side against it. Lena had eleven cards on fairness, on why a borrower who kept a book for a month owed something to the people waiting for it. She had two more on what the fees paid for.

Westbrook's first speaker, a tall boy named Arjun Pell, spent less than a minute on fairness. He talked instead about books that went missing. In towns that had dropped their fees, he said, more books came back, because people who owed a large fine had simply stayed away from the library, and the books had stayed home with them. He named one town and gave its figures for one year. Lena flipped through her cards twice, and then a third time, faster. Her hands had gone cold. She turned the stack face down on the table.

Tomas wrote two words at the top of his flow, circled them twice, and slid the sheet across to her: WHO PAYS? Below them an arrow ran to his note on Arjun's figures, where he had written 1 town, 1 yr.

When her turn came, Lena stood up holding the flow instead of the cards. She said that one town in one year was a small foundation for a rule meant for every library in the state. Then she asked who would pay for the books that still went missing, and for the copies bought to replace them, once the fees were gone. Her voice shook for the first sentence and had steadied by the third. She ran four seconds past her time, and when the timekeeper raised the red card she kept going until she had finished her point.

Carver lost on a two-to-one decision. On the bus home Lena read the ballots. The judge who had voted for Carver had written one line across the bottom of the ballot: Second speaker, strongest rebuttal of the day, once the cards went down. Tomas read it over her shoulder and said nothing for most of a mile.

At practice the following Tuesday she brought her cards, banded and numbered as always. But she had left the back of every card blank, and before the first round she asked Tomas to lend her a pen.

and when, and how far down, and when.

carrying a branch, a bottle, a raft of foam
down to the sea, as it has done for longer
than there has been a bridge, or a town.

laid across the water from bank to bank,
comes upstream against everything the river is doing,
and the river lets it.

for a channel that narrows like a funnel,
water climbing on its own back. All true.

turning slowly, as if it had remembered something
it left upriver.

a little longer than the evening needs,
and the water beside the road runs seaward
as if it had never once been turned.

My grandfather measured his land in paces. When a neighbor asked how long the north fence was, he would walk it, counting under his breath, and come back with a number: two hundred and twelve. Measuring with the body is the oldest way there is, and its weaknesses are easy to list. A foot, a forearm, a hand's width: each varies from one person to the next, and so for anything bought or sold, people eventually agreed on a single foot, kept somewhere official, against which every other foot could be checked. The Romans set their mile at a thousand double steps; the word mile comes from the Latin for a thousand.

And yet I have come to think the pace survived for a reason. It is the one measuring tool a person cannot leave at home. A tape measure is in a drawer when you need it; your legs are with you. What I am really doing is comparing one place to another using a ruler only I carry.

Official measures are agreements among strangers, and strangers need them. But between me and the bus stop, there is no stranger to satisfy. My grandfather understood that. In June 1881 the American ship Jeannette, which had been trapped in the Arctic pack ice for nearly two years, was crushed and sank north of the coast of Siberia. Three years later a handful of objects from the wreck turned up on an ice floe off the southwest coast of Greenland, on the far side of the Arctic Ocean.

To the Norwegian scientist Fridtjof Nansen, the objects were evidence. They could hardly have flown; something must have carried them, frozen into the ice, across the top of the world. If a current could do that to a few scraps from a wreck, Nansen reasoned, it could do it to a ship. He proposed to build one, let it freeze into the ice north of Siberia on purpose, and ride the drift.

Many experienced polar sailors thought the plan would kill him. Ships caught in pack ice were squeezed until their hulls gave way, as the Jeannette's had. Nansen's answer was the shape of the hull. His ship, the Fram, was built short and broad with a rounded bottom and smooth sides, so that ice pressing in from both sides would find nothing to grip and would push the ship upward instead of crushing it.

In September 1893 the Fram was frozen in, as planned, north of the New Siberian Islands. When the pressure came, the ice slid beneath the rounded hull and lifted the ship, as Nansen had hoped. For nearly three years the Fram moved with the ice, generally westward, while the crew took soundings, recorded the weather and measured the ice. It came free north of Spitsbergen in August 1896, having crossed a large part of the polar sea.

Two findings of the voyage were surprises. The first came from the soundings. Many geographers had expected the sea near the pole to be shallow, perhaps dotted with land that no one had yet seen. The Fram's lines went down more than three thousand meters, which showed a deep ocean basin instead.

The second came from comparing two of the crew's records: the direction of the wind and the direction in which the ship actually moved. The ice did not drift straight downwind. Day after day it moved off at an angle, roughly twenty to forty degrees to the right of the direction the wind was blowing. Nansen passed the puzzle to a Norwegian colleague, and it reached a young Swedish physicist, Vagn Walfrid Ekman, who published an explanation in 1905. The spinning of the Earth, Ekman showed, turns moving water in the Northern Hemisphere to the right, and each layer of water beneath the surface is turned a little farther than the layer above it.

The Fram never reached the pole; the drift carried it to within a few hundred miles. But a voyage designed to test one idea about the ice ended by raising another, and the pattern Ekman described, now called the Ekman spiral, is still taught to students of the ocean.

If a current could do that to a few scraps from a wreck, Nansen reasoned, it could do it to a ship. He proposed to build one, let it freeze into the ice north of Siberia on purpose, and ride the drift.

Many experienced polar sailors thought the plan would kill him. Ships caught in pack ice were squeezed until their hulls gave way, as the Jeannette's had. Nansen's answer was the shape of the hull. His ship, the Fram, was built short and broad with a rounded bottom and smooth sides, so that ice pressing in from both sides would find nothing to grip and would push the ship upward instead of crushing it.

Day after day it moved off at an angle, roughly twenty to forty degrees to the right of the direction the wind was blowing.
